lines: Watch what doesn't happen here. A new table appears inside a schema that was already tagged restricted, and nobody opens an editor to write it a rule.
It inherits the row filter and the column mask the instant it exists. A design built on per-table grants would have left this exact table briefly ungoverned.
Before I answer, think about the timing problem. The policy was written before this table existed. For it to apply the moment the table appears, it can't be checking the table's name.
So what is it actually checking?
answer: A tag, checked live, every time — not a list someone has to keep updating.
The policy was never written against this table specifically. It was written against a label, and anything carrying that label is covered the instant it's looked at.

lines: Two levels gets you one namespace per account, full stop. Watch what the third level buys: prod and staging sitting in the same metastore without a single name colliding.
That third level isn't decoration. It's the only reason two environments can coexist at all.
Don't file these under one heading called data. A table is rows and columns. A volume is a folder of files governed the same careful way. A function and a model get permissioned individually too.
A catalog scoped only to tables can't touch any of the other three.
This isn't a claim — it's run against a real permission tree. One grant, at the schema, reaches a table that already existed and a table created after, identically.
Notice what never happens: nobody goes back to grant it a second time.
Watch this carefully, because it's easy to get backwards. The policy checks the tag, not the family tree — so a table with no tag yet is not covered, even sitting right there in a tagged schema.
Only once the tag itself is actually inherited does the policy start applying. The tag is the trigger, not the location.
Here's the part worth sitting with: neither of these lives behind a separate dashboard you have to go hunting through.
Lineage down to the column, and every access logged — both are just tables. You query them the same way you'd query anything else.
Two different problems that look alike from a distance. Federation reaches into another system live, for your own people, governed exactly like a native table.
Delta Sharing goes further: someone with no account on your platform at all reads your table, carrying nothing but a bearer token.
If you only remember one line: a tag, checked live, is what makes governance apply itself — before anyone writes a rule for the specific object.
Three levels, four kinds of securable, one grant that never needs repeating, and a recipient who needs nothing but a token.
Before I answer, notice what's missing from this scenario: no shared account, no shared platform, nothing in common at all between you and this partner.
Can they still read your table?
answer: Yes. The protocol names the recipient as a principal holding a bearer token, full stop.
The server hands back pre-signed file URLs or temporary cloud credentials — neither one asks what platform the recipient happens to run.
